title: The Size of Every Subtree

concept.title: Process the nodes in reverse level order: children are finished before their parents
body: The *subtree* of a node is the node together with everything below it. Its size is `1 + the sizes of the subtrees of its children`. A recursive function computes this directly, but a tree of 20000 nodes can be a path, and a recursion that deep is not safe. The same computation can be done **without recursion** by processing the nodes in the right order.

List the nodes in **breadth-first order** (the root, then its children, then their children, and so on). In this list every node comes **after its parent**. So walking the list **backwards** meets every node **before its parent**: when a node is reached, all of its children have been handled and its size is final, and it can be added to the size of its parent.

body.code:
order = [root]
for v in order:                       # the list grows while we walk it
    order.extend(kids[v])

size = [1] * (n + 1)
for v in reversed(order):
    if parent[v] != 0:
        size[parent[v]] += size[v]      # v is final, pass it up

body: This "BFS order, then backwards" pattern replaces a post-order recursion in many tree problems (heights, sums, counts, tree dynamic programming) and works for any depth.

statement: A tree has `n` nodes numbered 1 to `n`. For every node its parent is given (0 for the root). For every node print the number of nodes in its subtree (the node itself and all nodes below it).
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n).
The second line has `n` numbers: for each node its parent, and 0 for the root.
outputFormat: One line with `n` numbers: the subtree size of the nodes 1, 2, ..., n.
constraints: The numbers describe one tree: exactly one node has the parent 0, and following parents always reaches it.
A parent can have a larger number than its child.
The tree can be a long path (depth up to n - 1).

examples.note: The root 1 has 6 nodes in its subtree, node 2 has 3 (2, 4, 5), node 3 has 2 (3, 6), the others 1: 6 3 2 1 1 1.

hints: Build the children lists and list the nodes in breadth-first order.
Every node comes after its parent in that list, so go through it backwards.
When you reach a node, its size is final: add it to the size of its parent.

explanation: The nodes are listed in breadth-first order and processed backwards, so every node is final before its parent; each node adds its size to its parent. No recursion is needed.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
par = list(map(int, input().split()))

kids = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
root = 0
for v in range(1, n + 1):
    p = par[v - 1]
    if p == 0:
        root = v
    else:
        kids[p].append(v)
order = [root]
for v in order:
    order.extend(kids[v])
size = [1] * (n + 1)
for v in reversed(order):
    p = par[v - 1]
    if p != 0:
        size[p] += size[v]
print(*size[1:])
